lines.text: For most of history, the world was impossibly large. This is the story of how we learned to cross it — and how, for a while, the journey itself became the destination.
It begins, improbably, at a temperance rally. In 1841 Thomas Cook charters a train for a day trip — and accidentally invents the package tour. Travel starts to belong to everyone.
In 1869 the Suez Canal opens, slicing thousands of miles from the route to the East. Suddenly the world is smaller, and the age of global travel has truly begun.
1883: the Orient Express departs Paris for the edge of Europe. Velvet, mahogany, candlelit dining — proof that a journey could be as glamorous as any destination.
By the turn of the century, steam and steel turn the Atlantic into a stage. Great liners race between continents, and crossing the ocean becomes a spectacle of luxury.
In 1907 the Mauretania crosses the Atlantic in just four and a half days — a record that will stand for thirty years. The true queens of the sea.
The new century builds the grandest ships ever seen — floating cities of ambition and elegance. Their story is also a reminder that progress always carries risk.
Then we look up. In 1927 a lone pilot flies nonstop across the Atlantic, and the world senses the future of travel might not float at all — it might fly.
The 1930s are the golden twilight of the liner. Ships like the Queen Mary carry ballrooms and grand staircases across the sea — luxury at full steam, just as the skies begin to beckon.
1939: great flying boats lift the first paying passengers across the ocean. Days at sea become hours in the air. The age of the airliner has arrived.
In 1952 the world's first jet airliner enters service. Travel gets faster, higher, impossibly modern — and the distances that once took weeks begin to vanish.
And in 1970 the jumbo jet opens the skies to everyone. What was once the privilege of the wealthy becomes a ticket within reach of millions.
Today the whole world is barely a day away. We cross oceans before lunch and forget how astonishing that is — yet every journey still carries the romance of those first travelers.
A century of travel. The journey continues. Where will you go next?
